result: Dentition is highly conserved in salamanders and caecilians with no cases of complete edentulism. All 65 salamander species examined have teeth on the lower jaw and palate, though some species lack upper jaw teeth. All 30 caecilian species examined possess teeth on all jaw elements.
evaluation: Claims C2, C30-C34, and C85-C89 provide comprehensive microCT data from 65 salamander and 30 caecilian species showing consistent presence of teeth across all examined specimens. The data directly support the conclusion that dentition is invariably present in these amphibian groups, with only minor variation in specific tooth-bearing elements in salamanders.

result: Teeth have been lost at least 22 independent times in frogs, representing a much higher frequency of edentulism than any other vertebrate group. Ancestral state reconstruction using reversible-jump MCMC indicates the ancestral state of Anura was toothed, with 134 of 429 examined frog species being edentulous across 19 families.
evaluation: Claims C3, C35-C43, C64-C65, and C97 present robust phylogenetic analyses using appropriate Bayesian methods on 524 amphibian species. The ancestral state reconstruction with high posterior probability (0.99) and comparison with literature-documented edentulous vertebrate lineages (8 other lineages) strongly support the conclusion that frogs exhibit exceptional frequency of tooth loss.

result: Maxillary and premaxillary teeth of the upper jaw evolve synchronously in frogs, being coordinately present or absent in all examined species. Vomerine teeth are more variable, present in 202 and absent in 226 species. All anurans lack dentary teeth except Gastrotheca guentheri.
evaluation: Claims C25-C29 and C92 present clear microCT data from 429 frog species showing coordinated presence/absence patterns for maxillary and premaxillary teeth (present in 292, absent in 136 species), with only two exceptions noted. The data directly support the synchronous evolution pattern and the exceptional nature of lower jaw tooth retention in G. guentheri.

result: Vomerine tooth loss does not always precede complete edentulism in frogs. The all-rates-different model was the best fit (AICw = 0.91) for three dental states evolution, and stochastic character mapping shows similar transition rates to edentulism from fully toothed (10.3) and toothed upper jaw with vomerine loss (13.8) states.
evaluation: Claims C44-C48 and C94-C96 present appropriate model comparison using AIC weights and stochastic character mapping on 425 anuran species. The all-rates-different model strongly outperforms ordered models (AICw = 0.91 vs. 0.00-0.06 for alternatives), providing robust evidence that vomerine tooth loss is not a prerequisite for complete edentulism and that upper jaw and palate dentition are independent modules.

result: Edentulism in frogs is strongly correlated with a microphagous diet specializing on small invertebrate prey. BayesTrait analysis shows the dependent model is strongly supported over the independent model (Bayes factor = 54.32), with 54 of 69 microphagous species being edentulous compared to 25 of 199 generalists.
evaluation: Claims C5, C49-C54, and C98-C100 present appropriate phylogenetic comparative analysis using BayesTraits on 268 frog lineages with diet data. The Bayes factor of 54.32 strongly supports correlated evolution (threshold >2), and the pattern holds across multiple dataset configurations (BF = 26.28 and 16.0 for reduced datasets). At least 16 of 22 independent tooth loss events contain microphagous species, providing convergent support.

result: Complete tooth loss in frogs is significantly associated with shortening of the lower jaw. Phylogenetic logistic regression shows a significant relationship (p<0.001), with edentulous species having an average relative jaw length of 83% versus 99% in toothed species.
evaluation: Claims C6, C55-C58, and C105-C107 present appropriate phylogenetic logistic regression on 423 anuran species with morphometric data. The highly significant p-value (<0.001) and substantial difference in mean relative jaw length (83% vs. 99%) provide strong statistical support for the association between edentulism and jaw shortening.

result: There is no significant relationship between complete edentulism and body size across all frogs (p=0.09). However, when excluding bufonids, a significant relationship emerges (p=0.015). Edentulous and toothed species span similar size ranges, and miniaturized species can be either toothed or edentulous.
evaluation: Claims C7, C59-C63, and C130-C134 present phylogenetic logistic regression results on 423 anuran species showing no significant relationship (p=0.09) between edentulism and body size. The conditional relationship when excluding bufonids (p=0.015) is appropriately noted and suggests clade-specific effects. The data on miniaturized species (13 toothed, 12 edentulous among 25 taxa ≤15mm SVL) support the lack of a general size constraint.

result: Frogs have a much higher occurrence of edentulism than any other vertebrate group. Literature review identifies only 8 other extant edentulous vertebrate lineages: no chondrichthyans, 3 actinopterygian fish lineages, and 5 amniote clades (3 mammal lineages, birds, and turtles).
evaluation: Claims C4, C64-C74 combine the study's phylogenetic data showing at least 22 independent tooth losses in frogs with a comprehensive literature review of edentulous vertebrates. The comparison is well-documented with appropriate citations and clearly demonstrates that frogs exhibit exceptional frequency of tooth loss compared to all other vertebrate groups.

result: Teeth were independently lost in the common ancestors of Bufonidae and Microhylidae. In Bufonidae, teeth have not been regained, but in Microhylidae, six reversals to toothed states were inferred. The nature of these reversals (true teeth vs. odontoids) requires histological investigation, though some taxa show evidence of true dentition.
evaluation: Claims C118-C125 present ancestral state reconstruction results showing independent losses and potential reversals. While the loss events are well-supported, the interpretation of reversals in Microhylidae is appropriately cautious. The authors acknowledge that re-evolution of true teeth is unlikely (C122) and hypothesize some structures may be odontoids (C123), but provide morphological evidence for true teeth in some taxa (C124-C125). Histological investigation is needed to definitively resolve the nature of these structures.

result: The majority of edentulous frogs are restricted to Bufonidae and Microhylidae. All 48 examined bufonid genera and 48 of 54 microhylid genera lack teeth. These two families comprise 18% of all frog species (1,334 of ~7,300 species).
evaluation: Claims C114-C117 present clear microCT data showing the concentration of edentulism in two diverse families. The taxonomic data from AmphibiaWeb (2021) appropriately contextualizes the diversity of these families. The findings are well-supported by the comprehensive sampling (48 of 48 bufonid genera, 48 of 54 microhylid genera examined).

result: Tooth formation occurs ontogenetically late in frogs (during or after metamorphosis) compared to other vertebrates, and this delayed odontogenesis may be linked to the evolutionary lability of teeth in anurans. The dentary bone ossifies relatively late in frogs and nearly always lacks teeth, while salamanders and caecilians always retain mandibular dentition.
evaluation: Claims C82-C85 combine established developmental knowledge (supported by citations to Davit-Béal et al., 2007; Lainoff et al., 2015; Harrington et al., 2013) with the study's microCT data showing consistent presence of mandibular teeth in salamanders and caecilians. The hypothesis linking delayed odontogenesis to tooth lability (C83) is appropriately presented as speculative but is supported by the comparative developmental and phylogenetic patterns.

result: Living pipid frogs have lost teeth twice independently: in the ancestor of Hymenochirus + Pseudhymenochirus and in Pipa. All Xenopus species and three of seven Pipa species retain teeth. Fossil evidence from Rhinophrynidae supports independent tooth loss in pipids and rhinophrynids.
evaluation: Claims C145-C148 integrate ancestral state reconstruction results with fossil evidence and taxonomic data. The inference of two independent losses in living pipids is supported by the phylogenetic analysis, and the fossil evidence from Rhadinosteus (toothed) appropriately supports the hypothesis of independent losses in Pipidae and Rhinophrynidae.

result: Among genera with dental variation, diet data are only available for Physalaemus and Engystomops. In both genera, edentulous species have specialized microphagous diets compared to toothed congeners that consume a broader array of invertebrates.
evaluation: Claims C126-C127 appropriately note the limited diet data available for genera with dental variation and cite Narváez and Ron (2013) for the dietary differences between edentulous and toothed congeners. This provides within-genus support for the broader pattern of association between edentulism and microphagy.

result: Dietary alkaloid sequestration has evolved as a predator defense mechanism in at least five clades of frogs that specialize on eating ants and mites, and teeth have been lost in several of these lineages including Dendrobatinae, Ameerega, Pseudophryne, Mantella, and Melanophryniscus.
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are well-supported by multiple citations documenting alkaloid sequestration in specific frog lineages (Saporito et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2002; Daly et al., 1997; Hantak et al., 2013). This provides additional ecological context linking microphagy, tooth loss, and chemical defense strategies.

result: The loss of teeth may be associated with evolution of secondary feeding apparatus. Nearly all frogs have a specialized tongue used in feeding, which might have facilitated repeated tooth loss. However, three pipid genera are both tongueless and edentulous but use suction feeding.
evaluation: Claims C75-C79 present a hypothesis about secondary feeding structures facilitating tooth loss, supported by citations (Davit-Béal et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2017; Regal and Gans, 1976). The exception of tongueless, edentulous pipids with suction feeding (Dean, 2003; Cundall et al., 2017) is appropriately noted and demonstrates that multiple feeding mechanisms can be associated with tooth loss.

result: Frogs, ants, and termites evolved at roughly the same time with important diversification events during the Cretaceous and Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, suggesting the repeated evolution of edentulism in frogs may be linked to the spatiotemporal diversification of ants and termites. Teeth have been repeatedly reduced in other tetrapods specializing on ants and termites.
evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by appropriate citations documenting the timing of diversification events (Moreau and Bell, 2013; Bourguignon et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2017) and parallel tooth reduction in other ant/termite specialists (Reiss, 2001; Daza and Bauer, 2015). The hypothesis of linked diversification (C103) is appropriately presented as speculative but is supported by the temporal coincidence and convergent patterns.

result: Shortened jaws in microphagous frogs result in altered feeding biomechanics, with faster symmetric feeding cycles compared to asymmetric cycles in long-jawed species. At least four lineages have evolved specialized muscular hydrostatic tongues, and microphagous frogs have relatively small eyes, suggesting the evolution of microphagy may have influenced multiple cranial traits.
evaluation: Claims C108-C113 are well-supported by citations documenting feeding cycle differences (Gans and Gorniak, 1982; Emerson, 1985), specialized tongue morphology (Trueb and Gans, 1983; Nishikawa et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2004), and eye size reduction (Thomas et al., 2020). The synthesis suggesting coordinated evolution of multiple traits (C113) is appropriately presented as a hypothesis but is supported by the convergent patterns.

result: Several edentulous vertebrate lineages show molecular tooth decay in genes critical for dentin and enamel formation. In bufonids, amelogenin is pseudogenized and likely became inactivated 40-60 million years ago. The authors hypothesize tooth-specific genes have degenerated repeatedly across edentulous anurans by novel inactivating mutations.
evaluation: Claims C151-C154 are supported by appropriate citations documenting molecular tooth decay in various vertebrate lineages (Meredith et al., 2009, 2013, 2014; Lin et al., 2016) and specific findings in bufonids (Lu et al., 2021; Shaheen et al., 2021). The hypothesis of repeated degeneration (C155) is appropriately speculative but is consistent with the pattern of repeated independent tooth losses documented in the phylogenetic analyses.

result: There appears to be no size-related constraints promoting complete tooth loss across all vertebrates. The smallest known vertebrate (microhylid frog P. amauensis) and the largest (blue whale) are both edentulous, demonstrating edentulous species span the entire spectrum of vertebrate body sizes.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 present an inference based on the observation that edentulous species span extreme body sizes. This is supported by established knowledge about P. amauensis (Rittmeyer et al., 2012) and blue whales, and is consistent with the study's finding of no general relationship between edentulism and body size in frogs (C60).

result: No stem tetrapods or fossil salamanders/caecilians have been described as edentulous. Stem salientians (Prosalirus, Vieraella, Liaobatrachus) had upper jaw teeth. Triadobatrachus lacks dentary teeth, and absence of lower jaw dentition is considered a synapomorphy of Salientia.
evaluation: Claims C135-C140 are supported by appropriate citations to paleontological literature (Ruta et al., 2003; Anderson et al., 2008; Matsumoto and Evans, 2017; Shubin and Jenkins, 1995; Báez and Basso, 1996; Gao and Wang, 2001; Ascarrunz et al., 2016; Milner, 1988). The fossil evidence appropriately contextualizes the evolutionary history of tooth loss in amphibians.

result: Several extinct crown-group anuran genera are edentulous, mostly hypothesized pipids. Extinct edentulous pipids likely represent two or more instances of tooth loss, though molecular phylogenies do not support the morphology-based clades. Tooth loss in pipids likely occurred at earliest during the mid-Cretaceous based on toothed early Cretaceous pipimorph fossils.
evaluation: Claims C141-C144 appropriately synthesize fossil evidence with phylogenetic analyses, citing relevant paleontological literature (Báez and Harrison, 2005; Trueb et al., 2005; Irisarri et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2017; Báez et al., 2021). The authors appropriately note the conflict between morphological and molecular phylogenies and the need for re-evaluation of fossil placements.

result: Two edentulous, non-pipoid fossil frogs from the late Cretaceous (Theatonius from Wyoming and Tyrrellbatrachus from Alberta) likely represent two independent cases of tooth loss and possibly the oldest record of edentulism in nonpipid frogs.
evaluation: Claims C149-C150 are supported by citations to Fox (1976) and Gardner (2015). The hypothesis that these represent independent losses and possibly the oldest nonpipid edentulism is appropriately attributed to Gardner (2015) and is consistent with the phylogenetic uncertainty about these fossils.

result: The developmental genetics of tooth formation in amphibians is almost entirely unexplored compared to understanding of chondrichthyan, teleost, and amniote odontogenesis.
evaluation: Claim C156 is supported by citations to comparative odontogenesis literature (Fraser et al., 2004; Tucker and Sharpe, 2004; Thiery et al., 2017) and appropriately identifies a major knowledge gap. This contextualizes the need for future developmental genetic studies in amphibians.

result: Data were collected from high-resolution microCT of over 500 of the 562 currently recognized amphibian genera, representing comprehensive taxonomic sampling across amphibian diversity.
evaluation: Claim C24 describes the extensive sampling effort (>500 of 562 genera) that forms the foundation of the study. The Methods section provides detailed protocols for microCT scanning and data processing, and Dataset S1 documents the specimens examined. This represents exceptional taxonomic coverage for a comparative study.

result: At least one species of Thorius possesses a novel sexually dimorphic dental polymorphism where males lack maxillary teeth but females maintain several teeth on the maxilla. This is the only known case of sexually dimorphic presence/absence dental polymorphism in an amphibian.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by citation to Hanken et al. (1999) and the authors' knowledge of amphibian literature. The uniqueness claim (C91) is appropriately qualified as being based on the authors' knowledge and represents an interesting exception to typical dental patterns.

result: Two species of Telmatobius are reported to have intraspecific variation in the presence or absence of dentition.
evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by citation to Barrionuevo (2017) and represents an interesting case of dental polymorphism within species. This is appropriately noted as exceptional variation within the genus Telmatobius.
